items.passage:
When a delivery rider in Bengaluru logs into an app at seven in the morning, she is not starting a job in any sense that labour law recognises. She is, in the language of the platform, activating herself as an independent partner. The distinction matters enormously, because it decides who pays for the petrol, who bears the cost of an accident, and who is entitled to a minimum wage. Platforms argue that flexibility is the whole point: riders choose their hours, accept or decline orders, and work for several apps at once. Critics reply that the freedom is largely an illusion, because the algorithm sets the price of every order, decides which rider gets which job, and can deactivate a rider whose ratings fall, all without any hearing. 
The debate is not new, but it has sharpened because the numbers have grown so large. India now has several crore gig workers, and most of them are in delivery, ride-hailing and domestic services. Their earnings swing wildly with weather, festivals and fuel prices, and surveys repeatedly find that a large share earn less than the local minimum wage once fuel and vehicle costs are counted. Yet the same surveys find that many riders prefer platform work to the alternatives available to them, which are often casual daily-wage jobs with no flexibility at all. This is the uncomfortable core of the issue: platform work can be both exploitative and, for the worker, the best option on offer. 
Governments have tried several answers. One approach is to reclassify gig workers as employees, which gives them the full protection of labour law but risks pushing platforms to hire far fewer workers and to schedule them rigidly. A second approach is to create a third category, a worker who is neither employee nor fully independent, with portable benefits such as accident insurance and a pension contribution that follows the worker across platforms. A third approach leaves the classification alone and regulates specific harms: minimum per-order pay, transparent deactivation rules, and a right to appeal. Each approach has a cost. Reclassification is clean in theory and disruptive in practice. A third category is flexible but invites endless litigation about where its boundary lies. 
The most promising path, several recent reports argue, combines the second and third approaches. Give gig workers a portable benefits floor funded by a small levy on each transaction, so that protection travels with the worker rather than depending on any single platform. At the same time, require platforms to disclose how their algorithms assign work and set pay, and to give a written reason before deactivation, with an appeal to a human reviewer. Transparency changes the balance of power: a rider who can see why she was passed over can challenge it. The levy, meanwhile, is small enough per order that it does not destroy the business model, yet large enough across crores of orders to fund real insurance and pensions.
None of this will happen by itself. The honest conclusion is that there is no solution that makes everyone better off at once. What is possible is a bargain in which workers gain a floor of security, platforms keep the flexibility that makes the model work, and consumers pay a little more for a service whose true cost is currently borne by the rider's body, her vehicle and her future.

Privacy: a digital rupee would protect users from surveillance
items.passage:
A central bank digital currency sounds like a small technical change: the same rupee, in digital form, issued directly by the Reserve Bank instead of by a commercial bank. In practice it rearranges the plumbing of money, and the rearrangement matters. When you hold cash, you hold a direct claim on the central bank. When you hold a bank deposit, you hold a claim on a commercial bank, which the central bank merely backstops. A retail digital rupee would give ordinary people a direct claim on the central bank in digital form, for the first time, without needing a bank account. Central banks have therefore moved carefully, piloting wholesale versions for banks first.
The case for a digital rupee rests on three arguments. The first is inclusion: crores of Indians still lack easy access to digital payments, and a central bank wallet could reach them without the fees and minimum balances of a bank account. The second is efficiency: settling payments in central bank money removes layers of intermediaries, which should make transfers cheaper and faster, especially across borders. The third is sovereignty: if private digital currencies or foreign payment systems become the rails on which Indians transact, the central bank loses its grip on monetary policy. A public digital currency is, on this view, a defensive move as much as an innovation, a way of keeping the rupee at the centre of the payment system as cash fades.
The case against is equally serious. If people can hold digital rupees directly with the central bank, they may move deposits out of commercial banks in a crisis, turning a bank run into a single tap on a phone. Banks would then have less deposit funding to lend, and credit would become scarcer or dearer. Privacy is the second worry: a central bank that can see every transaction holds a power that cash never gave it, and the line between fighting fraud and watching citizens is thin. The third worry is simpler and more mundane: a system run by the state may simply work worse than the private systems it replaces. 
The Reserve Bank's answer to these objections has been design, not denial. It has proposed holding limits on digital rupee wallets, so that no one can park large sums in central bank money and drain the banks. It has proposed tiered anonymity, with small transactions visible to nobody and large ones subject to the same checks as bank transfers. And it has proposed a two-tier model in which banks distribute the digital rupee and handle customers, while the central bank only issues it. Each of these is a compromise, and each compromise blunts one of the original benefits. A two-tier model keeps banks in the picture but reintroduces the very intermediaries the currency was meant to bypass.
The honest assessment is that a digital rupee will succeed or fail on the details of these compromises, not on the idea itself. If the limits are set too low, nobody will use it. If they are set too high, banks will feel the drain in the first crisis and demand a reversal. If the privacy design is not believed, people will stay with cash and private apps, whatever the official incentives. The technology is the easy part. The hard part is building a set of rules that ordinary people trust, that banks can live with, and that the state can operate without abusing. That is a political and institutional task, not a technical one, and it will take longer than any launch date suggests.

Neither conclusion I nor II follows

Neither conclusion I nor II follows

items.explanation: Let the number who do all three be x. Then exactly two is 2x, and at least two is 2x + x = 3x = 30, so x = 10 and exactly two is 20. Everyone is accounted for by only-one (20 + 25 + 15 = 60), exactly-two (20), all-three (10) and none, so none = 120 - 60 - 20 - 10 = 30. Using the exactly-two count, or the all-three count, or adding the all-three count to the answer, gives the other options.
items.question: In a group of 120 students in a class, 20 do only Hindi, 25 do only English and 15 do only French. The number who do exactly two of the three is twice the number who do all three, and 30 do at least two of the three. How many do none of the three?

items.explanation: The students doing only one subject number 30 + 25 + 20 = 75, and 40 do none, so those doing at least two number 150 - 75 - 40 = 35. Of these, 10 do all three, so those doing exactly two number 35 - 10 = 25. The at-least-two total 35 and the all-three count 10 are the traps.
items.question: Among the 150 students in a class, 30 do only Hindi, 25 do only English and 20 do only French, and 40 do none of the three. 10 students do all three of Hindi, English and French. How many do exactly two of Hindi, English and French?

Those who do Hindi in total are the only-Hindi group (40), the exactly Hindi and English group (25), the exactly Hindi and French group (15) and the all-three group (15), which is 40 + 25 + 15 + 15 = 95.

The third option separates them: where only the ban changed, scores did not rise, and where only tutoring changed, they did, so the rise tracks tutoring, not the ban. Students liking the ban says nothing about scores, a rise elsewhere could have a different cause, and the cost of the ban is irrelevant to whether it caused the rise.
options: Students said they liked the ban.
Scores also rose at a school that did not ban phones.
Classes that banned phones but had no tutoring showed no rise, while classes with tutoring rose whether or not phones were banned.
The ban cost the school nothing to enforce.

Consider the following statements. (1) Both finals were played in India. (2) India won exactly one of the two finals. (3) The 2023 World Cup final was played at Narendra Modi Stadium, Ahmedabad.
